connector: Hello! I’m Diana Barry, and I live at Orchard Slope, just over the brook from Green Gables. I’ve heard a girl has come to live with the Cuthberts, and I’m nearly wild to meet her. There isn’t another girl near enough to play with, and my sister’s too little. Mostly I read. Mother says I read far too much. A friend would fix that. Come and see.

a.raw: diana and anne promised to be friends forever they joined hands
a.fixed: Diana and Anne promised to be friends forever. They joined hands.
a.why: Capital letters on the names Diana and Anne, a period to end the first thought, a capital T to start the next sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: diana dropped her book the callers had come in
b.fixed: Diana dropped her book. The callers had come in.
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on the name Diana, a period where the first thought ends, a capital T to start the next sentence, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say whether the big words are showing off, or armour, and how you can tell.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what Diana gets out of the vow, since she already has a family.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say whether you think Marilla is right, wrong, or both, with one detail to back it up.

match.solemn: Solemn is about how serious a moment is. Picture two girls swearing a promise. Look for the meaning about being serious.
match.resolute: Resolute has resolve inside it, the feeling of having made up your mind. Look for the meaning about being firm.
match.enraptured: Enraptured has rapt inside it, carried away. Look for the meaning about great joy.
match.vindictive: Vindictive is about wanting to pay somebody back. Look for the meaning about revenge.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Diana Barry, and I’m your guide today, for the first time. Your question is about how a friendship starts, and you won’t find it in speeches. You’ll find it in small things people do, mostly with their hands. So watch hands. In word study you’ll be finding the words for things you can’t pick up. And there’s a poem to learn by heart. Say it out loud, not in your head.
transcripts.wgrd: This one’s like a game, and I love games. Pick something small that happens, the smaller the better. Then keep asking, and then what? Follow it in your head. When the chain seems to run out, push once more, because the last link is usually somebody who wasn’t even there when it started. If you can follow it all the way to what somebody is hoping for by the end, you’ve done it.
transcripts.dol: The model is somebody talking, so look at the marks that hold the talking in, and at what sits inside the last one. The sentence you’re fixing isn’t talking at all. It’s two whole ideas squashed together with nothing between them. Read it aloud and listen for where your voice drops. That’s where the first idea needs a period and the next one needs a capital letter. And two names want capitals too.
transcripts.guide1: Word study! First there are word parts to match, and one of the four isn’t a front part at all, so read the meanings carefully. Then the same four words as yesterday, then a sentence to tap, then a row of words to say out loud. Saying words out loud helps more than you’d think. Do the four boxes in order, and don’t rush the last one because it looks easy.
transcripts.morphology: Tap a word part, then its meaning. Before you tap, look at the three example words in brackets after each meaning and say them. If the part you’re holding fits at the front of all three, that’s your match. One of the four isn’t a front part at all. It goes at the end of a word, and its meaning is a thing, not a direction. Match that one last and it’ll nearly match itself.
transcripts.vocabulary: You met these four yesterday. Before you tap anything, say each word and try to picture the sentence it came from. Do the two you remember best first. Then there are only two words and two meanings left, and you can test each pair by saying them together and listening. If you tap a wrong one, a little line comes up to explain. Read it properly. It’s there to help, not to scold.
transcripts.grammar: Tap every one, and there’s more than one. Here’s my test. For each naming word, ask: could I put it in a box and carry it over to Green Gables? If I could, leave it alone. If I couldn’t, because it’s a feeling or an idea, tap it. Be careful. Things you could carry sit right next to the ones you can’t. Read to the very last word.
transcripts.spelling: You’re after the odd ones out, so don’t tap the words that do the usual thing. Say each word slowly, then quickly. In most of them one syllable goes soft and muddy. Those are the ordinary ones. Leave them be. The ones you want stay clear at both ends however fast you say them. Say each one twice before you decide. Then pick one you tapped and explain it in the box.
transcripts.guide2: I’m at home with a book, which is where I usually am. Mother thinks I read too much, and Father keeps giving me more. This week’s watch is about letting yourself look forward to things. I’m good at that. I’m not so good at the waiting. As you read, notice what somebody lets herself hope for, and how she behaves while she waits. Waiting badly and waiting well look very different.
transcripts.read: There’s one stop, after the first chapter, before you go on to the second. It asks what a promise means to somebody who has never had a family to promise her anything. When you get there, think about it from the other side, too. What would a girl who does have a family get out of a promise like that? Then read the second chapter straight through and count the things she looks forward to.
transcripts.rwm: Well. That’s me in there, and it’s true, I do. I never noticed till I read it. Try this: read the two sentences, then cover the second one with your finger. With just the first, I laughed once. Put the second back, and I’m a person who laughs. When you write yours, make the habit match who your character is, not just any old habit. Mine tells you I’m not much of a worrier.
transcripts.guide3: So now you know. She asked me straight out if I could like her enough to be her bosom friend, and I said I guessed so. Then we joined hands over the garden path, pretending it was a stream, and swore. I got the giggles, but I meant it. And I’ve been explaining ice cream to her, which is harder than it sounds. Go on. Say what you noticed, and show it from the book.
transcripts.chapter: The first question is about something she said to Mother when we met, and I was sitting right there. Why would a person use such big words at a moment like that? For the second, look at the ceremony, not just the promise. Who set it up, and why so grand? The third is about something Marilla said to her at home. I wasn’t there. Read it carefully and decide whether Marilla is right.
transcripts.wordconn: Your grammar answer is saved. You tapped the words for things you can’t put in a box. Well, I’ve just got one of those. Friendship. You can’t hold it, but you can watch it: two hands joined over a path, a promise said twice, a book lent. Look back at the word you wrote about and ask what somebody would have to do to show it. That’s how a writer makes an invisible thing visible.
transcripts.workshop: Today you sort walls: a person, a rule, or a fear. Here’s something I only found out afterwards. Anne was frightened of meeting me. She thought I mightn’t like her. That was her wall, and it was inside her the whole time. So when you pick your kid’s main wall, check whether it’s really a person, or a fear wearing a person’s face. Then add a smaller wall of a different kind.
